sermon.title: The Impact of the Gospel In Relationships Pt. 12
sermon.speaker: Jacob Lannom

commentaryIndex.title: Romans 12: Gospel-Shaped Harmony and Shared Work
commentaryIndex.commentary: God has also given us a shared work. Our gifts and responsibilities may look different, but our purpose is the same: to glorify Him. Each part of the church matters, and we ought to ask whether our service contributes to its harmony or adds conflict that does not need to be there.

commentaryIndex.title: Romans 12:17: Biblical Examples of Nonretaliation
commentaryIndex.commentary: Scripture gives us living examples of this choice. Joseph had the authority to punish the brothers who sold him, yet he considered what was right and used his position to preserve their lives, recognizing God's hand in his circumstances. David could have killed Saul in the cave, but he listened to his conscience, respected what was right before the Lord, and restrained his men from attacking. Stephen, even as he was being stoned, prayed for his attackers rather than calling for their destruction. None of these examples makes the evil done to them acceptable. They remind us that another person's wrongdoing never gives us permission to stop obeying God.

commentaryIndex.title: Romans 12:18: Peace without Surrendering the Truth
commentaryIndex.commentary:
Paul's instruction is clear: if it is possible, as far as it depends on us, we are to live at peace with everyone. We cannot control another person's heart, attitudes, or choices. That is why Paul says "if possible." But those words are not an excuse for being difficult, combative, or careless with people. As far as the responsibility belongs to us, we should be a people who pursue peace. If there is no peace, may it not be because we were the ones determined to create conflict.

This command comes right after Paul's charge not to repay evil for evil. When somebody wrongs us, it doesn't suddenly become right for us to do wrong back. The rest of the passage tells us not to take private revenge and to answer the needs of an enemy with good. The gospel changes what we do when someone treats us badly. We have to consider what is right before God, not merely what would feel satisfying in the moment.

At the same time, peace does not mean surrendering what God has spoken. There will be occasions when another person refuses peace because of our allegiance to Jesus Christ. We do not have to deny the truth of the gospel to avoid disagreement. But standing firm in truth and treating people with hatred are not the same thing. Religious violence and hostility are not the mission Christ has given His church. We are called to love people, show compassion, and speak the good news to our neighbors, including people who do not share our faith. Their greatest need is the same need we had: Jesus Christ.

Now bring the verse home. Where are we causing needless tension in a family, a friendship, a workplace, or a church? Are we too comfortable living in conflict? Think about a group of musicians playing distinct parts of one piece. Their instruments and responsibilities are different, yet they work together in harmony. God has given His people different gifts and forms of service, but our shared purpose is to glorify Him. This is not a demand that everybody be identical; it is a reminder that each of us must do our part faithfully. So ask yourself the question Paul places before us: as much as it depends on me, am I a source of peace or a source of conflict?

commentaryIndex.title: Genesis 45:1–8: Joseph Chooses Preservation over Revenge
commentaryIndex.commentary:
Joseph had every human reason to be angry with his brothers. They had hated him, sold him, and caused suffering that he could not simply undo. Now, when they came before him needing food, the balance of power was completely different. Joseph held a position in Egypt from which he could have used his authority against them. Instead, the passage shows his tears, his willingness to identify himself to them, and his concern to preserve life.

Joseph did not pretend his brothers' actions were harmless. He named what they had done. But he also saw that God had worked through those painful years to preserve his family during a famine. His brothers' evil intentions did not become righteous because God accomplished something good. Rather, Joseph refused to allow their wrongdoing to set the standard for his response. He considered what was right before the Lord.

When we are wronged, revenge can seem almost natural. We rehearse what was done to us, and we imagine what we might do if the opportunity came. Joseph's example presses us in another direction. Will we use whatever influence or opportunity we have to wound somebody back, or can we respond with mercy and seek what truly brings life? God can be at work in circumstances we would never have chosen. Our calling is not to repay evil with evil but to do what is right.

commentaryIndex.title: 1 Samuel 24:3–7: David Refuses an Easy Revenge
commentaryIndex.commentary:
David was fleeing from Saul, who had pursued him and sought his life. Then Saul entered the very cave where David and his men were hiding. Humanly speaking, the opportunity could hardly have been more convenient. David's men urged him to act, and it would have been easy to tell himself that removing Saul was the quickest way out of danger.

Yet David's conscience troubled him even after he cut a piece from Saul's robe. Saul's wrongdoing did not erase the fact that he was the Lord's anointed king. David refused to stretch out his hand against him, and he restrained the men who were ready to follow a different path. An open door is not automatically a command from God. We must ask not only what we can do but what is right in God's sight.

This is where our own hearts need examination. Someone can treat us unjustly, and we may have the perfect chance to embarrass them, punish them, or give them what they gave us. But the fact that vengeance is within reach does not make it obedience. David could have returned evil for evil. Instead, he chose restraint. We should be governed by God's Word rather than by our anger, pride, or a crowd encouraging us to strike back.

commentaryIndex.title: 1 Samuel 24:16–19: Good Answers a Wrongdoer
commentaryIndex.commentary:
When David finally spoke to Saul, Saul himself had to acknowledge the difference between his own wicked treatment of David and David's good treatment of him. Saul recognized that David had an opportunity to kill him and had let him leave safely. The one who had been pursuing David was now confronted with the righteousness of the man he had wronged.

I want us to see the effect of that decision. David's men watched a leader refuse revenge when revenge was available. Saul heard a testimony that exposed his own behavior without David having to murder him. That does not mean Saul's tears guarantee that every conflict was permanently healed. It does mean the choice to do what is right can speak more powerfully than striking back.

When we are tempted to justify retaliation, consider the witness we bear. We may not get an apology, and the other person may not change. But we can still make the righteous choice entrusted to us. Doing good is not the same as declaring evil acceptable. It is choosing not to become the wrongdoer ourselves.

commentaryIndex.title: Acts 7:54–60: Stephen Prays While Being Stoned
commentaryIndex.commentary:
Stephen was not facing a mild disagreement. His opponents were enraged by his witness, drove him out, and stoned him. Even as they killed him, Stephen called upon the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and asked that their sin not be held against them. He did not answer their hatred with his own curse.

That kind of response forces us to examine how we react to much smaller injuries. We can carry bitterness over a careless remark or decide to get even over a slight. Stephen was suffering violence for his testimony about Christ, yet his last prayer sought mercy for those hurting him. The power of the gospel is seen in a heart that can pray while being wronged.

There is a beautiful connection here to the Lord Jesus. At the cross, Jesus prayed for forgiveness as He suffered. Later, Stephen followed that example. We should never imagine the Christian life means pretending persecution and wrongdoing are good. Rather, we see a servant of Christ who trusted his Lord, bore witness faithfully, and refused to surrender his heart to revenge. This is the kind of Christlike response Paul's words in Romans 12 call us to pursue.

commentaryIndex.title: Luke 23:34: Christ Prays for His Enemies
commentaryIndex.commentary:
At Calvary we see more than an example of patience. We see the Savior suffering at the hands of sinful people and, praying for those responsible. If anyone had authority to call down judgment on His enemies, it was Jesus Christ. Yet He did not answer the cruelty of the cross with personal retaliation.

We have to remember who was hanging there. Jesus did not come simply to teach us to be nicer to difficult people. He gave Himself for sinners. His suffering and sacrifice are the foundation of the forgiveness we need, because apart from Him we were the ones in need of mercy. What He accomplished at the cross makes the gospel the good news we carry to people who may even oppose us.

When I am tempted to repay evil for evil, the cross calls me to look again at the Lord's mercy. His prayer does not tell us that cruelty is righteous or that justice does not matter. It shows a Savior who can offer forgiveness in the midst of hatred. We are not Christ, and we cannot save anybody by our suffering, but because we belong to Him, we can respond with compassion and point people toward the forgiveness He offers.

scriptureConnections.rationale: Part of one nonretaliation and peacemaking argument; v.17 frames v.18
Private revenge is refused while active good toward the enemy is commanded
Joseph’s treatment of brothers demonstrates good rather than revenge, in narrative context
David refuses to exploit a chance to injure Saul and restrains his companions
Saul’s words confirm David’s righteous restraint later in the same chapter
Stephen’s response under violence resembles Jesus and embodies nonretaliation
Stephen asks mercy for his killers after Jesus’ crucifixion prayer; parallel is thematic, not chronological prophecy
Peace with God through justification is distinct from, but ethically related to, peaceful behavior toward others
Earlier exhortations to bless persecutors and practice humility inform “with all people”
